name: Under-ice swimming

card.summary: Swimming in ice-covered or near-freezing water, taken up as a winter cold-exposure practice that enthusiasts link to leanness, mood, recovery and a healthier-looking complexion.
card.note: Cold shock, hypothermia and cardiac events are documented causes of death in cold-water immersion; swimmers with heart or blood-pressure conditions face higher risk.

quick.overview:
Under-ice swimming belongs to the wider tradition of winter and ice swimming, where people enter water through a hole cut in ice or swim in water colder than about 5 degrees C. Enthusiasts in looksmaxxing and wellness circles associate regular cold exposure with a leaner body, better mood and energy, and recovery that supports training.

Research on ice swimmers is mostly small case studies and observational work: changes in body temperature, blood markers, bone-metabolism hormones and the exercise hormone irisin after swims. A narrative review reports that regular, graded cold swimming in healthy experienced people appears to bring health benefits, alongside a risk of death in unfamiliar people.
quick.how: Practitioners swim in lakes or sea inlets in winter, often in clubs, with a cut hole or spring-fed spot kept open. Competitions under the IISA and IWSA use water below 5 degrees C with a limited swimsuit and cap [1]. Many build up gradually through autumn, swim short durations and warm up afterward, often in a sauna in Nordic and Baltic traditions.
quick.risks: Cold shock causes an involuntary gasp and rapid breathing that can lead to inhaling water, and cold-induced arrhythmia can cause cardiac arrest; these are the most common causes of death in cold-water immersion [1]. Hypothermia develops more slowly and alcohol speeds its onset. People with heart, lung or blood-pressure conditions, young children and older adults are advised to take particular caution [1].

lead: Under-ice swimming is swimming beneath or through a surface of ice, usually in the form of winter or ice swimming in water close to 0 degrees C. It is a tradition in Nordic, Baltic and Eastern European countries and is tied to sauna culture in Denmark, Estonia and Finland [1]. Wikipedia places records of ice swimming in Russia as early as 1525, with the Epiphany dip and Polar Bear clubs such as Coney Island (founded 1903) among its better-known forms [1].

People adopt it for appearance-adjacent reasons: staying lean, reducing puffiness and a refreshed look, better mood and more consistent training. A body-composition study of 81 ice swimmers found that circulating irisin, a hormone associated with exercise and cold, fell after swimming and that the size of the change was related to body-fat characteristics rather than muscle parameters [2].

Competitive ice swimming grew in 2009 with the creation of the International Ice Swimming Association and the 'Ice Mile', 1,608 m in water below 5 degrees C [3]. Ice swimming was a demonstration sport at the 2014 Winter Olympics in Sochi [3].

chain: Cold stress and exercise raise energy use and mood
Practitioners hope for leanness, recovery and a fresher look
angle.text: Practitioners swim in ice water hoping to support leanness, recovery and mood that carry through to training and appearance. Studies measure blood markers and body composition in swimmers rather than looks directly.

paras: Winter swimming takes place outdoors in cold season water; where water freezes, ice swimming involves a hole cut in the ice or a spring-fed spot that stays open [1]. Under IISA and IWSA rules, competitors swim in water typically below 5 degrees C, often on a 25 m course, with goggles, a single bathing suit and a latex or silicone cap; neoprene is not allowed [1]. Holes are kept open with circulation pumps or covers, and heated mats limit slippery surfaces [1].

Ice swimming is a traditional part of life in northern Europe and, according to Wikipedia, dates in Russia to 1525 [1]. The Orthodox Epiphany immersion on 19 January declined under the Soviet Union and revived after the 1990s, with about 2 million people across Russia in January 2020 [1]. Louis Sugarman was a famous ice swimmer in the 1890s, Geneva's Coupe de Noël has run since 1934, and Jinan, China, has hosted winter swimming festivals since 2014 [1]. The IISA was founded in 2009 [3].

Wikipedia summarises studies in which winter swimmers reported less stress and fatigue, more vigor and better mood and memory, along with pain relief for some conditions and fewer upper respiratory infections [1]. A 2020 narrative review concluded that cold swimming by experienced, healthy people in a regular, graded and adjusted mode appears to bring health benefits, while unfamiliar swimmers risk death from cold shock or hypothermia [4].

A case study of a swimmer completing six Ice Miles within two days recorded metabolic acidosis and increases in blood glucose, cortisol and creatine kinase after each swim [3]. A case study of a multiple world-record holder exposed to -5 to -37 degrees C for 50 days found testosterone up by about 60 percent and lower white blood cell counts [6]. Studies of 87 regular ice swimmers aged 42 to 84 examined bone-metabolism markers after swims [7], and a related study examined sclerostin and meteorin-like protein [8]. A performance analysis of IISA events looked at anthropometric characteristics [9].

The cold shock response and cardiac arrhythmia are the most common causes of death in cold-water immersion, and hypothermia sets in more slowly, with exhaustion possible within 15 minutes in some estimates [1]. A 2025 case report described persistent coronary microvascular dysfunction in an ice swimming champion after a coronary procedure [10].

Published work consists mainly of small observational studies and case studies in ice swimmers, covering core temperature, blood chemistry, bone markers and irisin [2][3][6][7][8]. No controlled trial has tested ice swimming for body composition, skin or other appearance outcomes.

timeline.event: Earliest Russian records of ice swimming cited by Wikipedia [1].
Coney Island Polar Bear Club founded [1].
